items.abstract: Predictive maintenance (PdM) for industrial assets is increasingly expected to support not only clean-test discrimination, but also compact inference, calibration-oriented probability quality, interpretable behaviour, perturbation-aware evaluation, and reproducible reporting under deployment constraints. This paper evaluates a reliability-aware compact artificial intelligence (AI) framework across the AI4I and MetroPT PdM datasets. The framework compares nine pre-specified compact model families, namely residual multilayer perceptron (ResMLP) Lite, gated recurrent unit (GRU) Lite, autoencoder (AE) Classifier Lite, PhysicsGate multilayer perceptron (PhysicsGate MLP), PhysicsGate AE Classifier Lite, BufferEnsemble PhysicsGate, PhysicsCrossGate ResMLP, Ablation BufferEnsemble NoGate, and Ablation BufferEnsemble NoBuffer, producing eighteen model-dataset pairs. Evaluation covers F1 score, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), precision-recall area under the curve (PR-AUC), Brier score, parameter count, inference latency, reliability-summary rows, perturbation behaviour, and Integrated Gradients (IG) attribution where applicable. The results do not support a single universal best model. Instead, residual, recurrent, AE-classifier, physics-guided gated, ensemble, and ablation variants exhibit dataset- and metric-dependent trade-offs, with some models favouring discrimination and others favouring calibration-oriented probability quality, compactness, or attribution-supported inspection. The PhysicsGate variants are therefore framed as lightweight magnitude-aware gates rather than physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), and IG is interpreted as model-specific attribution rather than causal fault diagnosis. The accompanying Code Ocean capsule provides a reviewer-facing source-code and smoke-test validation package for the released workflow.
title: Reliability-Aware Compact AI Framework for Industrial Predictive Maintenance Under Deployment Constraints

items.abstract: <jats:p><div class="htmlview paragraph">The task of visual inspection has important safety and cost implications, but studies of visual inspection reliability are still rare. If we are to understand and improve reliability, then techniques and insights are needed from different disciplines. Three disciplines are reviewed for their potential contributions: Non-Destructive (NDI) reliability studies, industrial inspection studies and CRM/MRM studies. Examples of how the use of multiple disciplines can help measurement and analysis are given, reaching the conclusion that more explicit integration among these disciplines is required.</div></jats:p>
title: Human Factors and the Reliability of Airframe Visual Inspection

items.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Sandia National Laboratories conducted an experiment for the National Nuclear Security Administration to determine the reliability of visual inspection of precision manufactured parts used in nuclear weapons.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Visual inspection has been extensively researched since the early 20th century; however, the reliability of visual inspection for nuclear weapons parts has not been addressed. In addition, the efficacy of using inspector confidence ratings to guide multiple inspections in an effort to improve overall performance accuracy is unknown. Further, the workload associated with inspection has not been documented, and newer measures of stress have not been applied.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Eighty-two inspectors in the U.S. Nuclear Security Enterprise inspected 140 parts for eight different defects.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Inspectors correctly rejected 85% of defective items and incorrectly rejected 35% of acceptable parts. Use of a phased inspection approach based on inspector confidence ratings was not an effective or efficient technique to improve the overall accuracy of the process. Results did verify that inspection is a workload-intensive task, dominated by mental demand and effort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Hits for Nuclear Security Enterprise inspection were not vastly superior to the industry average of 80%, and they were achieved at the expense of a high scrap rate not typically observed during visual inspection tasks.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Application:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides the first empirical data to address the reliability of visual inspection for precision manufactured parts used in nuclear weapons. Results enhance current understanding of the process of visual inspection and can be applied to improve reliability for precision manufactured parts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Visual Inspection Reliability for Precision Manufactured Parts
